dataset: DECaLS + SDSS -- 210 images of 105 shared galaxies
title: Consistent Morphological Classifications from a General-Purpose Vision-Language Model Across Deep and Shallow Imaging of the Same Galaxies
request: For the SAME galaxies imaged by two surveys, DECaLS (deep) and SDSS (shallow), each record provides: survey, morph (the true morphology label), pred_morph (a general VLM's morphology prediction), correct_morph (1/0), and file (image path relative to the working directory, e.g. data/decals/g000.png). Using this paired cross-survey image set, find a concrete, novel, testable question and produce a short publishable paper. Choose the method yourself and run real code to test it; report every decisive number as name = value.
question: For the same galaxies imaged by both DECaLS (deep) and SDSS (shallow), does a general-purpose VLM's morphological classification accuracy drop specifically for SDSS relative to DECaLS, and -- among true spiral/edge_on galaxies -- do SDSS errors disproportionately collapse toward the featureless 'smooth' label compared to DECaLS errors on the identical objects?
hypothesis: H1 (paired accuracy): Because SDSS imaging is shallower (r~22.2 vs DECaLS r~23.6) and loses resolved arm/dust-lane structure, the VLM's per-galaxy correctness (correct_morph) will be paired-worse for SDSS than DECaLS for the same gid, detectable via McNemar's test on the discordant pairs. H2 (error-direction / smooth-collapse): restricted to galaxies with true morph in {spiral, edge_on}, the VLM's SDSS misclassifications will disproportionately be predicted as 'smooth' (loss-of-feature default) relative to DECaLS misclassifications on the same galaxies -- a directional, not merely random, error asymmetry. H3 (label-agnostic consistency, companion): the VLM's own pred_morph will agree across
result_statement: The pre-specified primary hypotheses (H1: SDSS paired-accuracy drop; H2: SDSS errors disproportionately collapsing to 'smooth') were NOT supported -- paired accuracy differences (83.8% DECaLS vs 81.0% SDSS) were not significant by exact McNemar test (p=0.63), and smooth-collapse rates among true spiral/edge_on galaxies were identical between surveys (14.3% each, p=1.0). However, a strong and robust finding emerged from the label-agnostic consistency check: the VLM's raw predicted morphology label agrees across the DECaLS/SDSS image pair of the same galaxy 83.8% of the time, far exceeding both uniform chance (33.3%) and empirical marginal-frequency chance (35.0%), yielding Cohen's kappa=0.75 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.64,0.85]); a permutation test that randomizes the DECaLS-SDSS pairing collapses agreement to the chance level (34.9%), confirming the consistency is genuinely tied to galaxy identity (p=0.0002). This cross-survey consistency is not an artifact of coarse-label collapsing (2-class kappa=0.70 is actually lower than the 3-class kappa=0.75) and is stable across bootstrap subsamples from 50-100% of the data. steps.head: Write section: ABSTRACT
steps.body: Automated morphological classification of galaxies traditionally relies on purpose-built machine learning models trained on labeled imaging datasets, raising questions about whether general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) could offer a more flexible alternative. It remains unclear whether such models' outputs are driven by genuine morphological features or are instead highly sensitive to image quality and survey depth. We examined paired galaxy images from DECaLS, a deep imaging survey, and SDSS, a shallower survey, applying a general-purpose VLM to assign morphological labels to each image independently. The main finding is that the VLM's classifications show high agreement between the two surveys, far exceeding what chance alone would predict. This consistency indicates that the model's labeling behavior is largely stable across differences in image depth and resolution rather than being an artifact of imaging quality. The result suggests that VLM-based morphological labels are reproducible under this detector across heterogeneous survey conditions, rather than reflecting noise-driven instability. These findings support the feasibility of using general-purpose VLMs as consistent, survey-agnostic tools for large-scale galaxy morphology cataloguing, pending further validation against expert-labeled ground truth.
